A.W. Bhuiyan, Additional Attorney General, instructed by B. Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ---------- for the appellant. 
M.A. Jalil, Advocate-on-Record -------- for the respondent.
parties:
Province Of East Pakistan (Now Bangladesh)
Vs.
Syeduddin Ahmed
full_judgment:
Badrul Haider Chowdhury, J:—This appeal by special leave is directed against the judgment and order of the High Court Division in F.A. No.70 of 1964.

2. Bangladesh is the appellant. The respondent as plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration of his title to the suit land alleging, inter alia, that he was alloted 5 acres of Govt. Khas land from mouza Telikhali in 1958. The Settlement was made in Settlement case No.3 of 1958-59. It was duly approved by the Additional Collector and since then the plaintiff has been in possession of the said land. In 1962 the Board of Revenue, it is alleged, by an order dated 3-10-61 cancelled the settlement. Hence the suit.

3. The appellant contested the suit by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the respondent or the members of his family were not cultivators and he was therefore, not entitled to settlement of Government khas lands under the rules. The Board of Revenue was justified in cancelling the settlement.

4. Plaintiff examined three witnesses and the defendant did not examine any witness at the trial. The trial Court dismissed the suit mainly on the ground that the very basis of the settlement in favour of the plaintiff was lacking namely, the plaintiff was not a bonafide cultivator and since he did not come within the category of person to whom settlement could be given, such settlement was inoperative illegal, without jurisdiction and void abinitio and the same could not be binding against the Government. In this view of the matter the suit was dismissed.

5. On appeal the High Court Division in a carefully considered judgment noticed the kabuliyat Ext.3 and considered the contention whether the plaintiff respondent could validly claim settlement and the Board of Revenue had any authority for cancelling this settlement. Reliance was placed on two unreported decision of the High Court Division in F.A. No.33 of 1964 and F.A. No.226 of 1963. The learned Judges took the view that the Board of Revenue exercises administrative control but such power and control do not extend to cancellation of lease granted by a valid settlement. Ext.3 the Kabuliyat was considered and the view was, if the lessee had violated any of the terms of the lease, the Government could proceed against him for cancellation of the lease and his eviction from the land. In this view of the matter it was held that the Board of Revenue had no authority to cancel the lease granted by the Revenue Deputy Collector, Bakerganj which was approved by the Additional Collector. The Judgment and decree passed by the trial court are set aside and the suit was decreed.

6. Leave was granted to consider the question of correctness of decision given bb the High Court Division and whether the High Court Division erred in decreeing the suit on erroneous interpretation of the expression "bonafide cultivator".

7. Mr. A.W. Bhuiya, Additional Attorney General appearing for the appellant submitted mainly on the ground that the respondent plaintiff did not answer the description of bonafide cultivator and settlement was given by the District Authorities contrary to the direction given in the Government Estate Manual. The Board of Revenue cancelled the settlement in exercise of its power. The decree that has been passed by the High Court Division, therefore, requires to be reversed.

8. The plaintiff was an employee of the Bakerganj Collectorate. He stated in the plaint that he was granted settlement of 12'80 acres of agricultural lands under Mouza Char Acharya in 1952 but as the Char land was the subject matter of litigation he could not be given possession though he paid Salami and rent. He mentioned that in Misc. Case No. 699-R.A. dated 19-8-58, the then Commissioner Mr. W.B. Kadri, C.S.P. gave direction for settlement of some lands to the affected tenants of Char Acharya. He also prayed for settlement as he was affected tenant of Char Acharya. The Revenue Deputy Collector by his order dated 7.3.59 accepted the proposal for settlement of 5 acres of land with the plaintiff and accordingly direction was given to open a new Khatian in Register 1.

9. Ext.3 kabuliyat was executed by the plaintiff in favour of the Collector, Bakerganj. One of the condition of the kabuliat runs thus:

"Within three years from this date I shall stay in the land with my family by constructing suitable dwelling house within the boundary of this land of Kabuliyat. I shall not live in any other house. If I do so or I do not construct a good house or if I do not live on this land, then the Government shall eject me under section 44(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act. To that I shall not be entitled to raise any objection or I shall not be entitled to claim compensation or mesne profits".

Then again plaintiff stipulated:

"I shall cultivate land my-self or with the members of my family and I shall make the whole land cultivable within the period of this settlement If I do not cultivate the land then the Government shall eject me from this land after expiry of the period of this settlement in accordance with the provisions of the said Act."

10. In the written statement the Government took the stand that kabuliyat had not been signed either by the executor or by the recipient or by anybody, it does not bear any date of execution and the gaps in the 1st paragraph have not yet been filled up. Notwithstanding such assertion, it appears that the name of tenant was entered in Register II as a tenant and the plaintiff was given the possession of the land. The plaintiff paid salami as required and paid rent upto 1962. By Memo No.3191 AI dated 3-10-61 it seems the Board of Revenue cancelled the settlement of the plaintiff on the ground that the candidates of these cases were Collectorate staff and other staff who were serving in strategic positions which enabled them to get settlement for themselves by "exercising undue-influence" (Ext. E/2).

11. An appeal was preferred and it was disposed of by the Secretary, Revenue Department by its order dated 7-7-62. It was considered that the appellants were not entitled to settlement of the Government khas land and as such the settlement with them were not legal "though some of the petitioners claim that kabuliyats for the lands executed by them have been accepted by the Government thereby establishing a relationship of landlord and tenant between them and the Government, that stand is not correct because the Kabuliyats were not accepted by the Collector or an authorised agent of the case" and the order was passed. "The appeals are therefore failed on merit". Then the last paragraph mentioned: "Again, the orders for settlement of lands by the Collector in these were cancelled under Orders of the Governor and not under any order of the Board of Revenue and as such, no appeal is actually maintainable. The result is that the appeal petitions fail."

12. When the order of cancellation was passed the plaintiff was not given a show cause notice as to why his settlement shall not be cancelled. The cancellation order is dated 3-10-61 and by that time the plaintiff went into possession upon payment of salami and rent. The impression that was created was that the order was passed by the Board of Revenue and an appeal was preferred by the aggrieved settlement holders including the plaintiff but this appeal was also disposed of without giving any hearing to the plaintiff. In other words, at no stage the plaintiff was heard as to why his settlement shall be cancelled. This position has led him to file the suit. The learned trial court considered the evidence and came to the conclusion that plaintiff did not answer the description of a bonafide cultivator as mentioned in the Government Estate Manual. According to Government Memo No.12965- L.R. dated the 12-8-1957 certain principles regarding settlement of land have been laid down. Clause (3) reads as follows:

"Lands shall be settled only with a bonafide cultivator or a member of a family of a bonafide Cultivator who will cultivate the lands himself or get them cultivated by the members of his family".

13. It lays down the rule of priority as to who will get preference to get Government khas land: In this case the main objection of the Government is that the plaintiff was not a bonafide, cultivator. It was alleged in the order of cancellation that the plaintiff got the settlement by exercising "undue influence". Neither he was heard nor his appeal was disposed of after giving him any hearing. So the question of undue influence has not been substantiated. In the suit the plaintiff examined witnesses but the Government did not. Therefore the very basis that the plaintiff obtained settlement by .exercising undue influence appears to be lacking.

14. Leave was not granted to consider the question whether the Board of Revenue had authority to cancel the settlement. In passing it may be noticed that the Secretary, Revenue Department mentioned in his order that these settlements were cancelled "under orders of the Governor and not under any order o!' the Board of Revenue and, as such, no appeal is actually maintainable," (Ext.8/a). The learned Additional Attorney General mainly argued on the point that initially the settlement was bad because the plaintiff respondent was not a bonafide cultivator. He relied on clause (iii) of Rule 63 of the Manual which is quoted above.

15. Mr. Bhuiyan contended that the finding of the trial Court was that the plaintiff respondent was an employee of the Government and he was "by no means a bonafide cultivator" and concluded "the Board of Revenue was perfectly justified in cancelling the same which is definitely binding against the plaintiff". Section 76 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides for settlement and use of land vested in the Government and its assets: and says- "the Government shall be competent to make settlement of such land in accordance with such rules as it may make in this behalf or to use or otherwise deal with such land in such manner as it thinks fit."

Provided that no land shall be settled with a person unless he is a person to whom transfer of land can be made under section 90."

"Provided further that in making settlement of any cultivable land preference shall be given to an applicant for settlement who cultivates land by himself or by the members of his family". Section 78 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act gives the rule making power and clause(zt) provides for the rules for settlement of lands referred to in section 76. In section 82 'bonafide cultivator' is defined for the purpose of part V means "a person who cultivates lands by himself or by members of his family or by, or with the aid of servants or labourers or with the aid of partners or bargadars, and also includes on agricultural labourer;". The learned Additional Attorney General is correct in contending that this definition in section 82 in only for the purpose of that part and this definition is wider then the persons meant by the bonafide cultivator in rule 63(3). That rule is to be taken as principle to be followed in the matter of settlement of the Government khas land and it mentioned 'bonafide cultivator' and includes the "members of the family of such cultivator who will cultivate the land himself or get them cultivated by members of his own family". In other words, it excludes the servants or labourers or partners or bargadars or cultivator labourer. The idea is plain, namely, Government land should be settled with the bonafide cultivator or a member of the family of bonafide cultivator. The emphasis is on "who will cultivate the land himself or get them cultivated by the members of his own family". Ext.3 the kabuliat exactly speaks in the same terms: "I shall cultivate land myself or with the members of my family ". When in the kabuliyat members of the family are included, it is difficult to appreciate the judgment of the trial court when the evidence of P.W.3 Fazlul Hoque was brushed aside by observing: "I decide that Fazlul Huq simply looks after and manages the suit property under the plaintiff" and concluded that "Fazlul Huq the nephew of the plaintiff though allegedly resides with his maternal uncle the plaintiff cannot be member of his family". To say the least, those who are conversant with the family condition of our villages would not consider the assertion of P.W.3 Fazlul Hoque as something improbable when he says that he resides in the plaintiff's house and manages his property and also ploughs land.

16. "Member of family" is often defined: in some enactments as to who are/who are not members of the family. Those enactments specify the conditions of conferring certain privilege or liability with which they are to be saddled. For example: The alienation of Law (Distressed Circumstances) (Restoration) Ordinance, 1976 (XXVIII of 1976) provides for restoration of alienated land under certain circumstances and transfer of agricultural land with in the specified period shall be deemed to have been made for economic distress if the transferor and the members of his family do not own in the aggregate after transfer more than three acres of land. Section (3) says "for the purpose of this section 'family' in relation to a transferor, includes wife, son unmarried daughter" and excludes a class of people expressly.

17. In the land Development Tax Ordinance, 1976 (XLII of 1976) rate of tax is specified at 90 paisa for standard bigha if the land held by a family does not exceed 25 standard bighas and sub-section (5) of section 3 provides: "for the purpose of this section family is in relation to a person, includes such persons and his wife, son unmarried daughter, son's wife, son's son and son's unmarried daughters" and excludes an adult and married son who have been living in a separate mess.

<u>18. Thus it is clear that the expression `family' is to be understood in the light of the given enactment. In so far settlement of the khas land is concerned the expression 'Family' has not been used in definitive sense; the emphasis is only on the point that the land should be cultivated by himself or by member of the family. Evidence was led by the plaintiff that his nephew ploughed the land who resided with him. This evidence was not rebutted. Since this condition is satisfied it cannot be said that the plaintiff respondent did not answer the description of the person to whom settlement could be made.</u>

19. Next it is to be remembered that the settlement was made in 1959 and the kabuliyat was executed, rent and Salami have been paid, the kabuliyat was therefore acted upon. When the kabuliyat is acted upon, it created a jural relationship between the parties and one of the condition in the kabuliat is that "within 3 years he shall construct a dwelling house and shall not live in any other house". Then it says "if I do so or I do not construct a good house or if I do not live on this land, then the Government shall eject me under section 44(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act". Section 44(B) of the Bengal Tenancy Act is in the following terms:

"A non-occupancy raiyat shall subject to the provisions of this Act, be liable to ejectment on one or more of the following grounds, and not otherwise (namely):

(b) on the ground that he has used the land in a manner which renders it unfit for the purpose of the tenancy, or that he has broken a condition consistent with this Act and on breach of which he is under the terms of a contract between himself and his landlord, liable to be ejected.

But the lease was not cancelled on the aforesaid grounds. It was apparently cancelled because the plaintiff was not "a bonafide cultivator". The cancellation order was passed by the Governor and not by the Board of Revenue. This cancellation was done without following the principles of natural justice and the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit wherein he led evidence on all factual aspects namely (a) upon the proposal by the Revenue Deputy Collector the Additional Collector approved the settlement whereupon kabuliat was executed (b) before the expiry of 3 years the settlement was cancelled without observing the principle of natural justice; (c) positive evidence was led that the nephew of the plaintiff ploughed the land who lived with him as member of his family; (d) Government defendant did not adduce any evidence to rebut the claim of the plaintiff; (e) Jural relationship had been created by the execution of the kabuliat, (f) No proceeding was taken under section 44(B) for violation of the settlement condition; (g) payment of Salami and rent had been made and no complaint had been made of any default; (h) that the Governor cancelled the settlement whereas consistent stand was taken that it was a Board of Revenue who did it and the finding was recorded by the trial Court that the Board of Revenue had ample power so to do.

20. We have not heard on the point of power of the Board of Revenue in such matters especially in the matter of cancellation of settlement. It is clear from Ext.8(a) the order was passed by the Governor and not by the Board of Revenue. The observations of the High Court Division on this point need not be taken to have been approved by this judgment. The ratio of the decision rests on the point that at no stage, any investigation was made on the point that the plaintiff respondent was not a bonafide cultivator nor land was being cultivated by a member of his family. If such investigation is not done, as has not been done, the opinion is that the appeal preferred by the Government against the decision of the High Court Division decreeing the suit must be dismissed.

21. In the result therefore this appeal is dismissed. No costs.

End.
